title: Minimum Number of Removals to Make Mountain Array
summary: An array is considered a mountain array if it has at least three elements and there exists an index where the elements strictly increase to that index and then strictly decrease from that index.
statement: An array is considered a mountain array if it has at least three elements and there exists an index where the elements strictly increase to that index and then strictly decrease from that index. Given an integer array, determine the least number of elements to remove to convert it into a mountain array.
constraints: nums has 3 through 1000 positive integers and can be reduced to a strict mountain.
A mountain strictly increases to an interior peak and then strictly decreases.
Return the fewest removals while preserving relative order.
hints: For each possible peak, measure the longest strict rise ending there and strict fall starting there.
Compute LIS lengths from the left and mirrored LIS lengths from the right.
Only peaks with both lengths above one are valid; maximize left+right-1.
Every retained mountain has one peak and two such subsequences, while joining the best compatible sides at a peak creates a valid mountain.
editorial: Every retained mountain has one peak and two such subsequences, while joining the best compatible sides at a peak creates a valid mountain.

tests.explanation: The entire three-element array already strictly rises then falls, so no removal is needed.
A longest mountain has five elements, so three of the eight values must be removed.
